linkages: links between parents and their biological/adoptive children, used to identify the couple's first child
partners linked to each other through cohabitation, registered partnership or marriage records
female same-sex couples identified as couples where one partner is the birth mother and the partner is a woman (the 'social mother')
matched pairs created by Coarsened Exact Matching on the child's birth year, partners' ages and both partners' pre-parenthood labor earnings

sample.universe: the whole population of Denmark, Finland, Norway and Sweden in the register years covered
sample.unit_of_observation: couple-year, at event times -3 to +5 around the birth of the couple's first child
selection_rules: different-sex couples and female same-sex couples who had their first child together and who are cohabiting, in a registered partnership, or married
only couples where one partner is the birth mother of the child (children with two adoptive parents excluded)
exclude couples who had multiple births (e.g., twins)
exclude couples who did not live together at the time of the child's birth
all persons included had to have positive labor earnings the year before parenthood
both partners 20-55 years old at the time of having their first child
exclude couples if they separate in the year the child is born
exclude couples in which one of the partners dies and/or whose child died within the first year after birth
after the child is one year old, censor couples who separate and/or in which one of the partners dies
include parents who entered parenthood between 2002 and 2014 in Sweden, 2002 and 2015 in Denmark and Norway, and between 2002 and 2018 in Finland

sample.period: register data 1999 until 2016 in Sweden, 2017 in Norway and Denmark, and 2020 in Finland; first births 2002-2018 depending on country

construction_notes: Household earnings = all pre-tax wages and income from self-employment of both partners, top-coded at 1 million Euros.

Household earnings including social transfers add work-related transfers tied to parenthood (maternal, paternal and parental leave benefits, temporary parental leave in Sweden, cash-for-care benefits in Norway and Finland) plus sick leave benefits for both partners.
All earnings are before taxes, inflation-adjusted to 2014 levels and converted to euros at the 2014 currency rate (0.11 SEK/EUR, 0.12 NOK/EUR, 0.13 DKK/EUR).
Negative earnings are recoded as zero.
Couple type: different-sex couples = reference category 0, female same-sex couples = 1.
Event time: dummies for three years before to five years after the first child's birth, reference the year before birth.
Calendar-year dummies with 2014 as the reference category.
Birth mother's education in three categories: higher education, at most short-cycle tertiary (reference), missing.
Event-study coefficients rescaled as C_tk = alpha_hat_tk / E(y_hat | T = t, K_i = k) to give percentage changes relative to the predicted earnings in the absence of children.
Figures 2 and 3 plot household labor earnings in yearly 1000 EUR; Figure 1 plots the birth mother's share in percent.

claims.statement: In Denmark, the birth mother's share of household labor market earnings after the first child's birth is higher in female same-sex couples than in different-sex couples, i.e. different-sex couples specialize more.

treatment.label: Couple type: female same-sex couple versus different-sex couple

definition.value: Couple type is defined as different-sex couples (reference category 0) and female same-sex couples (1); the couple is identified from register links between the two cohabiting, registered or married partners who had their first child together, one of whom is the birth mother. The authors read couple type as a proxy for how equally the couple divides paid work and care.

timing.value: Fixed couple characteristic, measured at the birth of the couple's first child (event time 0).

outcome.label: Birth mother's share of household labor market earnings

definition.value: The birth mother's labor market earnings as a share of the couple's total labor market earnings, plotted in percent by event time from 3 years before to 5 years after the first child's birth. Labor earnings are all pre-tax wages and income from self-employment, top-coded at 1 million Euros, inflation-adjusted to 2014 levels and converted to euros at the 2014 rate; negative earnings are recoded as zero.

timing.value: Annual, event time -3 to +5 relative to the birth of the first child.

units.value: percent of household labor market earnings accruing to the birth mother

magnitude.interpretation: The paper gives no per-country number for the gap. For different-sex couples 'mothers contribute between 32% and 40% of the household earnings 5 years after the first child's birth' across the four countries, while same-sex couples' contribution is about .50.

estimand.target_population: First-time parental couples in Denmark meeting the sample restrictions (all couples, unmatched).
estimand.time_horizon: each year from 3 years before to 5 years after the birth of the first child; the paper highlights the gap 5 years after birth

population.description: Different-sex couples and female same-sex couples in Denmark who had their first child together between 2002 and 2015, were cohabiting, in a registered partnership or married, with one partner the birth mother, followed from 3 years before to 5 years after the birth (all couples meeting the sample restrictions).
population.ages: both partners 20-55 years old at the time of having their first child
population.selection: Couples where one partner is the birth mother (children with two adoptive parents excluded); multiple births and couples not living together at the child's birth excluded; couples separating in the birth year, couples where a partner died, and couples whose child died in the first year excluded; after the child is one year old couples who separate or where a partner dies are censored; all persons had to have positive labor earnings the year before parenthood

identification.source_of_variation: Comparison of two couple types that differ in how equally they divide paid work and care; the authors treat sexual orientation as exogenous to the specialization decision.

key_assumptions.assumption: Couple type is exogenous: sexual orientation is not influenced by the decision to specialize or by other factors that might predict household earnings, so female same-sex and different-sex couples can be compared directly.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Argued in the introduction (p. 3); no test is offered.

key_assumptions.assumption: The estimation sample is conditioned on survival of the couple: couples who separate in the birth year, where a partner dies or where the child dies in the first year are excluded, and after the child is one year old couples who separate or where a partner dies are censored; both partners had to have positive labor earnings the year before parenthood.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Sample construction described on pp. 9-10; note 1 records that separations are under-observed in Norway.

key_assumptions.assumption: Couples decide on their division of paid work and care with the aim of optimizing household income.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Conceded as an assumption in the discussion (p. 22); the authors note other motives (gender norms) may drive the division.

key_assumptions.assumption: In the unmatched comparison no observable differences between couple types are adjusted for, so the gap also reflects that same-sex couples are older, higher-earning and more highly educated before birth.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Table 2 and the motivation for matching (p. 10).

threats_discussed: Selection into being a same-sex or different-sex parental couple; same-sex couples are older, higher-earning and more highly educated before birth (Table 2).
Education cannot be matched on without too large a sample reduction for same-sex couples, so it is only controlled for.
Small same-sex samples, especially in the later years after parenthood, make significant differences harder to detect.
In Norway separated couples are only observed if they marry or have a child with a new partner, so separation is under-recorded (note 1).
Couples may divide work and care for non-financial reasons (gender norms), which the household-income framing does not capture.
robustness_checks: Coarsened Exact Matching on the child's birth year, partners' ages and both partners' pre-parenthood labor earnings (Table 3; Figures 3-5).
Event study repeated on the unmatched sample: 'results are very similar in the long run for the unmatched sample, results available upon request' (p. 19).
Analyses repeated excluding couples who had children before 2005 (Sweden) or 2009 (Norway) (note 2).
Sensitivity analysis on whether couples have a second child (note 3).
Figure 1 re-estimated for matched and unmatched samples (note 4).
Labor-earnings analyses replicated with household income including work-related social transfers (Figure 5).
unresolved_confounders: Birth mother's education is not matched on, only controlled for, because matching on it 'would lead to a too significant sample reduction for same-sex couples' (p. 10).

Selectivity into couple type beyond the matching variables: the models include no couple fixed effects and the authors say selectivity is taken into account only 'as much as possible' via matching (p. 14).
Non-financial utility (acting in line with gender norms) is not observed and may drive the division of work and care (p. 22).

estimator.value: Unconditional group means of the birth mother's earnings share by event time, plotted by couple type (no regression)

estimation.specification: Raw event-time means of the birth mother's share of household labor earnings, separately by couple type and country; four lines per panel (All DSC, All female SSC, Matched DSC, Matched SSC).

sample_n.value: 963 female same-sex couples (all), 877 (matched); 246,236 different-sex couples (all), 55,904 (matched)

mediators_claimed: differences in parental leave use and work-hour reductions between the partners

heterogeneity.finding: The gap persists after matching: 'Even when making couples as similar as possible by matching them, the within-couple earnings gap is larger for different-sex couples than for same-sex couples' (p. 16).

Finland is the only country with a within-couple earnings gap among same-sex couples (about 44% for the birth mother 5 years after birth, versus close to 50% elsewhere); the authors point to the Finnish home-care allowance.
For same-sex couples the gap 'is much more temporary and only discernable during the first two years after the birth of the first child' (p. 16).

ambiguities: Figure 1 prints no numeric values; the per-country size of the gap could not be transcribed, only its direction.

The N printed on Figure 1 for Finland (446 all / 421 matched female same-sex couples; 244,273 / 35,922 different-sex) differs from Table 2 and Table 3 (558 / 520 and 315,252 / 38,892); the reason is not stated.
